title: Freight broker myths: rates, margins and real service value
seoTitle: Freight broker myths: rates, margins and real service value
searchIntent: What do people misunderstand about freight brokers?
excerpt: A practical look at common assumptions about brokers, carrier rates and the work behind arranging transportation.
takeaway: Judge a broker by the work performed, the agreements made and the service delivered. A shipment margin alone does not explain profitability, and a low quote alone does not establish the best transportation option.

sections.title: What do people misunderstand about freight brokers?
paragraphs: Luis uses this lesson to challenge the idea that the broker’s role is simply taking a cut between a shipper and a carrier. Arranging freight involves customer development, carrier sourcing, communication, paperwork and handling exceptions. Doing those jobs poorly deserves criticism; doing them well provides a service.

The useful discussion is about what each party contributes and whether it keeps its commitments. Broad claims that all brokers or all carriers behave the same way do not help anyone manage a shipment.

sections.title: Who determines the rate on a shipment?
paragraphs: A rate is shaped by the requirements of the move, available capacity, timing and the parties’ negotiation. Brokers influence the quotes they offer and the loads they accept, but no individual broker controls the entire freight market.

Luis’s practical position is to question an unrealistic customer budget instead of passing the pressure along without thought. Confirm what the shipment requires and whether a capable carrier can perform it at the proposed price.

sections.title: Is the shipment spread the broker’s take-home profit?
paragraphs: The difference between the customer charge and carrier cost still has to support the business. Staff, systems, financing and other operating expenses affect what remains. Looking at a single load’s spread cannot tell you whether the brokerage is profitable.

That does not excuse poor service or broken agreements. Both parties need to understand their own costs, negotiate clearly and honor the terms they accept. A productive rate conversation is more useful than assuming what the other business must be earning.

sections.title: Is going direct always the better choice?
paragraphs: A direct carrier relationship can be a good fit. A capable broker may add value through broader sourcing, coordination and response when the original plan changes. Compare the actual service and total effort required for the shipment.

Ask who will handle replacement capacity, updates and unresolved documents. Then judge whether the provider delivers on that responsibility. Luis’s argument is for earning the margin through useful work, rather than expecting a customer or carrier to value the brokerage title by itself.
